title: Croatian hero hurt in transit scuffle
article: It is a long, downward spiral from being the model Croatian soldier, adored by a nation, to the critical-care unit of a Toronto hospital. Yesterday, Jasen Drnasin reached the nadir of that spiral.

Such is the unique trajectory of Mr. Drnasin's life that when the 32-year-old was sprayed with pepper foam by TTC constables on a city bus on Sunday -- it would eventually take three police officers and the two constables to subdue him -- and his heart momentarily stopped beating, it was arguably not the most extraordinary event in his bizarre personal history.

Years before his latest misadventure, Mr. Drnasin was a sort of national hero in Croatia, after he became the country's first citizen to graduate from New York's West Point, one of the most prestigious military academies in the world.
The fame quickly turned to infamy: A year after he graduated in 2000 and returned to Croatia, he was indicted on charges of attempted murder for stabbing his girlfriend while he was high on drugs.
The incident was one of the biggest news stories of the year in Croatia, and sparked a national discussion about drug use in the military.
On Sunday evening, two TTC special constables were dispatched to investigate a reported assault on a bus on Eglinton Avenue West at Royal York Road.

At around 9 p.m., they found Mr. Drnasin on another city bus in the west end of the city, according to Rose Bliss, a spokeswoman with the provincial Special Investigation Unit, which has been called in to review the incident.
She said a conversation between the constables and Mr. Drnasin escalated into a struggle, at which point they tried to subdue him with pepper foam.

However, Mr. Drnasin managed to get off the bus and began running along Eglinton. The police were called, and three officers tracked him to a grassy area, where they and the TTC constables subdued and handcuffed him.
Shortly afterward, Mr. Drnasin went into "medical distress," Ms. Bliss said. He was taken by ambulance to Humber River Regional Hospital in critical condition.
Speaking to CTV on Tuesday, his father, Anton Drnasin, said he didn't expect his son to survive the next 48 hours. Yesterday, however, Mr. Drnasin's condition appeared to be improving.
Mr. Drnasin was born in Croatia but spent most of his teenage years in Canada. Yesterday, the Croatian ambassador to Canada confirmed Mr. Drnasin has dual citizenship.

According to Croatian news reports, he returned to the country of his birth in 1991, at the age of 17, to fight in the war that erupted when Yugoslavia disintegrated. By most accounts, he was an extraordinary soldier.

In 1996, Peter Galbraith, the U.S. ambassador to Croatia, invited him to study at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point. A Croatian Defence Ministry delegation, Croatia's ambassador to the United States and about 30 Croats from the New York area attended Mr. Drnasin's graduation in 2000.
He would return to Croatia a national hero -- and to take command of the 4th guard brigade.

Early in 2001, Mr. Drnasin made headlines in Croatia again, this time charged with attempted murder. High on drugs, he had stabbed his girlfriend, Tanja Milanovic, about seven times in the chest and neck with a pocketknife.
It appears his military service in Croatia also left him with posttraumatic stress disorder.
Ms. Milanovic forgave Mr. Drnasin, and after he was released, they reunited and had a daughter.

Reached by phone yesterday, Anton Drnasin said he had been advised by lawyers and police not to speak to the media. However, he said that Ms. Milanovic and the couple's 18-month-old daughter are in Canada, having travelled here from Croatia after Sunday's incident.

It is still unclear why TTC officers had to use pepper foam on Mr. Drnasin. TTC constables do not fall under the SIU's jurisdiction, and it had not been confirmed whether the TTC will launch an investigation.
